Islam (part 4)

5 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Shi'a Muslims follow twelve Imams, and every mosque has an imam. Is that the same word for the same job?
  2. Mission 2Muslims have two great festivals each year. Why is one of them marked by a sacrifice?
  3. Mission 3No verse mentions a fruit you have never seen. Is a Muslim allowed to eat it?
  4. Mission 4Muslims live in every country and speak many languages. Can they really be one community?
  5. Mission 5Why are the first words a Muslim baby hears the same as the call to prayer?
Mission 1

Mission 1: Shi'a Muslims follow twelve Imams, and every mosque has an imam. Is that the same word for the same job?

Make a guess: Shi'a Muslims follow twelve Imams, and every mosque has an imam. Is that the same word for the same job?

Mission 1

One word, two meanings

  • Imam (Arabic) means "one who stands in front": a leader.
  • Every mosque has an imam: the person who leads the prayer and serves the community. Sunni and Shi'a mosques both have one.
  • For Shi'a Muslims, the Imams (capital I) are something more: leaders chosen by Allah from the Prophet's family to guide the ummah after him.
  • Belief in these Imams, Imamah (the imamate), is one of the Shi'a five roots of faith.
  • So the same word can mean a local prayer leader or a divinely chosen guide.
Mission 1

The imam in Sunni Islam

  • Origins: the Prophet led the prayer himself and told others who should lead in his absence.
  • Chosen by the mosque community for knowledge of the Qur'an and good character, often after years of study.
  • Not a priest: no special holiness, no ordination; any adult Muslim man with knowledge can lead the congregation; most schools allow a woman to lead other women. Only Allah forgives sins.
  • Prayer: stands in front, facing the qiblah; the congregation follows his movements.
  • Community: gives the Friday khutbah (sermon), teaches the Qur'an, counsels families, conducts marriages (nikah) and funerals.
  • In Britain many imams also work as chaplains in hospitals, prisons and universities.
Mission 1Read the source

Sahih al-Bukhari 73:34–37

  • 73:34: the Prophet held up two fingers together: he and the one who looks after an orphan will be as close as this in Paradise (paraphrase).
  • 73:35–36: one who works for widows and the poor is like a fighter in Allah's cause, or one who prays all night and fasts all day (paraphrase).
  • 73:37: young men stayed with the Prophet for twenty nights. He sent them home to teach their families, saying: pray as you have seen me pray; when prayer is due, one of you should call the adhan, and the eldest should lead (paraphrase).

Q1 According to 73:37, how is a prayer leader chosen?

Show answer

From among the group: here the eldest; no special class of priests.

Q2 What do 73:34–36 add to the imam's role?

Show answer

Leading the community in caring for orphans, widows and the poor.

Mission 1

The mu'azzin

  • The mu'azzin (CIE: Muʾazzin) calls Muslims to prayer five times a day with the adhan.
  • The first was Bilal, a freed slave of Ethiopian (Abyssinian) descent, chosen by the Prophet for his strong, beautiful voice.
  • Traditionally called from the minaret; a mu'azzin is chosen for a clear voice, correct Arabic and good character.
  • Significance: the adhan turns daily life towards Allah and gathers the community.
  • In many Shi'a mosques the adhan includes an extra line bearing witness that Ali is the friend (wali) of Allah.
Quick check
?Which statement about the imam of a Sunni mosque is accurate?
Mission 1Diversity

imam and Imam side by side

  • Sunni imam: chosen by the community · leads prayer, preaches, teaches · an ordinary believer with knowledge · many in every generation.
  • Shi'a prayer leader: the same role in Shi'a mosques, usually a trained scholar.
  • Shi'a Imam: appointed by Allah through nass (designation by the Imam before) · sinless and without error · the true interpreter of the Qur'an · twelve for most Shi'a (Twelvers), the last alive but hidden; a living Imam for most Isma'ilis (a smaller Shi'a group).
  • Different: for Shi'a Muslims, leadership of the ummah is a matter of faith (a root); for Sunni Muslims, a matter of practice and community choice.
Mission 1Evaluate

"The imam is the most important person in a mosque."

  • For: he leads every congregational prayer and gives the Friday khutbah. Muslims bring him questions about faith and family. He represents the mosque in the wider community.
  • Against: Islam has no priesthood: any qualified believer may lead (in mainstream practice a man for a mixed congregation), and each believer stands before Allah alone. The mu'azzin, teachers and the mosque committee are vital too. The worshippers, the ummah, are what the mosque is for.
  • Shi'a view: the most important leaders are the twelve Imams; a mosque's prayer leader serves under the guidance of senior scholars.
  • Judge it by: What is a mosque for? Could worship continue without the imam? Does "important" mean authority or service?
Mission check

?At a Shi'a mosque in Birmingham, a trained scholar leads the Friday prayer. A poster in the hall marks the birthday of Imam Ali al-Rida. A visitor asks: "Is the man leading prayer one of the Imams?" Which answer is most accurate?

"Imam" names two different things: a role any qualified believer can fill (in mainstream practice a man for a mixed congregation), and a divinely chosen guide in Shi'a belief.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Muslims have two great festivals each year. Why is one of them marked by a sacrifice?

Make a guess: Muslims have two great festivals each year. Why is one of them marked by a sacrifice?

Mission 2

Two Ids, one moon

  • Id (Arabic 'Id) means a festival: literally a day that returns every year.
  • Islam has two Ids that every Muslim group keeps:
  • Id-ul-Fitr: the festival of breaking the fast, at the end of Ramadan.
  • Id-ul-Adha: the festival of sacrifice, during the Hajj.
  • Both follow the lunar Islamic calendar, so they move about 11 days earlier each year in the solar calendar.
  • A new month starts when the new crescent moon is seen.
  • The Prophet set these two festivals in Madinah, in place of older festival days (hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, paraphrase).
  • Your spec spells them Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha.
Mission 2

Id-ul-Fitr: why Muslims celebrate

  • When: 1 Shawwal, the day after Ramadan ends.
  • Thanks: Muslims thank Allah for the strength to complete the fast.
  • The Qur'an asks fasting Muslims to "complete the period, and that ye should magnify Allah for having guided you, and that peradventure ye may be thankful" (Qur'an 2:185, Pickthall).
  • Remembering the Qur'an: Ramadan is the month the Qur'an was first revealed.
  • Purpose: joy after self-discipline; forgiveness; the whole ummah celebrating together.
  • Zakat-ul-Fitr (fitrah): a fixed gift of food, or its value, paid for each family member before the Id prayer, so the poor can celebrate too.
Mission 2

Id-ul-Fitr: how Muslims celebrate

  • Wash (ghusl), wear new or best clothes, eat something sweet such as dates.
  • Recite the takbir on the way: "Allahu akbar" (God is the Greatest).
  • Id prayer in congregation: two rak'ahs with extra takbirs, then a sermon. Held in mosques, halls or parks.
  • Greet: "Id Mubarak" (blessed Id). Embrace and forgive.
  • Visit family and friends; share a festive meal and sweets.
  • Children receive gifts or money; cards are sent.
  • Some families visit the graves of relatives and pray for them.
Quick check
?Why is Zakat-ul-Fitr paid before the Id-ul-Fitr prayer rather than at any time in the year?
Mission 2

Id-ul-Adha: Ibrahim's test

  • When: 10 Dhu al-Hijjah, the day pilgrims on Hajj sacrifice at Mina. Muslims everywhere join them.
  • Origin: the Qur'an tells how Ibrahim (Abraham) dreamed that Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son.
  • The son agreed. Both submitted to Allah. Muslims believe that at the last moment Allah stopped Ibrahim and provided a ram instead.
  • The Qur'an does not name the son. Most Muslims believe he was Isma'il (Ishmael).
  • Meaning: total submission to Allah, trust, and Allah's mercy.
Mission 2Read the source

"A clear test"

> "O my dear son, I have seen in a dream that I must sacrifice thee. So look, what thinkest thou? He said: O my father! Do that which thou art commanded. Allah willing, thou shalt find me of the steadfast." (Qur'an 37:102, Pickthall)

> "Lo! that verily was a clear test. Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim." (Qur'an 37:106–107, Pickthall)

Q1 How does the son respond to his father?

Show answer

He accepts Allah's command and promises to be steadfast.

Q2 What does "ransomed" tell Muslims about Allah?

Show answer

Allah did not want the boy's death: He tested obedience, then showed mercy by providing an animal.

Mission 2

Id-ul-Adha: how Muslims celebrate

  • Id prayer in congregation in the morning, with takbir.
  • Qurbani (Arabic udhiyah): a sheep, goat, cow or camel is sacrificed after the prayer, in Allah's name. A healthy animal of a set minimum age.
  • The meat is usually shared in three parts: the family, relatives and friends, and the poor.
  • Many Muslims pay for qurbani abroad through a charity, so meat reaches people in need.
  • Family visits, a festive meal, new clothes, gifts.
  • The Qur'an stresses the inner meaning: "Their flesh and their food reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." (Qur'an 22:37, Pickthall)
Quick check
?A Muslim teacher explains qurbani using Qur'an 22:37. What is the main point she would draw from this verse?
Mission 2Evaluate

"Id-ul-Adha is more important than Id-ul-Fitr."

  • For: Muslim scholars often call it the greater Id (al-'Id al-Kabir). It is joined to Hajj, a pillar of Islam. It remembers Ibrahim, a model of total submission. It lasts longer: qurbani may continue on the days after Id (to the 12th or, for some schools, the 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah).
  • For: the sacrifice is an act of worship in itself, and feeds the poor across the world.
  • Against: Id-ul-Fitr crowns a whole month of fasting, prayer and Qur'an reading. It is often the more widely celebrated festival in families, especially for children.
  • Against: the Prophet set both Ids together; each teaches a different side of Islam: gratitude after self-discipline, and submission after testing.
  • Judge it by: link to the Five Pillars? Which shapes daily life more? Which is celebrated more in Britain today? Can festivals with different purposes be ranked?
Mission check

?A Muslim nurse in Bradford is on shift on the morning of Id-ul-Adha. She cannot go to the Id prayer, but she pays a charity to sacrifice a sheep for her family and share it with refugees, and joins her family's meal that evening. Which part of the meaning of Id-ul-Adha does her charity payment show most clearly?

Two festivals, two lessons: thanks after the fast, and submission like Ibrahim's, each shared with the poor.

Mission 3

Mission 3: No verse mentions a fruit you have never seen. Is a Muslim allowed to eat it?

Make a guess: No verse mentions a fruit you have never seen. Is a Muslim allowed to eat it?

Mission 3

Halal and haram

  • Halal: permitted, lawful.
  • Haram: forbidden, unlawful.
  • These are rulings of shari'ah, the "straight path" of Islamic law.
  • They cover far more than food: drink, clothing, money, speech, relationships, work.
  • Starting point: most scholars hold that everyday things are halal unless forbidden. The list of haram things is short; the halal world is wide.
  • Significance: keeping halal is worship. Muslims believe the rules come from Allah, who knows what is good and harmful for people.
  • It also marks Muslim identity: a halal meal, a hijab or refusing a drink shows faith in public.
Mission 3

Where the rules come from, and five categories

  • Origins: the Qur'an; the Sunnah of the Prophet (hadith); and scholars, using agreement (ijma) and reasoning by analogy (qiyas).
  • Example of qiyas: the Qur'an forbids wine because it intoxicates, so scholars also forbid drugs that intoxicate.
  • The Prophet taught that the halal is clear and the haram is clear, with doubtful matters between them that the careful person avoids (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, paraphrase).
  • Scholars sort actions into five categories:
  • Fard or wajib (obligatory): e.g. the five daily prayers.
  • Mustahabb (recommended): e.g. extra prayers, giving sadaqah.
  • Mubah (neutral, simply allowed): e.g. choosing which fruit to eat.
  • Makruh (disliked): better avoided, but not sinful.
  • Haram (forbidden): sinful, e.g. drinking alcohol.
  • The first four all fall within the halal (permitted) in its wide sense.
Quick check
?Many Muslims say that "almost everything is halal". Which statement best explains why?
Mission 3Read the source

Forbidden foods

> "He hath forbidden you only carrion, and blood, and swineflesh, and that which hath been immolated to (the name of) any other than Allah. But he who is driven by necessity, neither craving nor transgressing, it is no sin for him." (Qur'an 2:173, Pickthall)

  • Surah 5:3 repeats this list and adds animals killed by strangling, beating, falling or goring, unless properly slaughtered (Qur'an 5:3, paraphrase).
  • "Immolated" means sacrificed or slaughtered.

Q1 Name the four forbidden foods.

Show answer

Animals that died by themselves, blood, pork, and meat offered to anything other than Allah.

Q2 When may a Muslim eat a forbidden food?

Show answer

Only under real necessity, such as starvation, and no more than needed.

Mission 3

Halal food in practice

  • Dhabihah (halal slaughter): a sane adult Muslim (many Sunni scholars also accept Jews and Christians) uses a very sharp knife, says Allah's name (bismillah, Allahu akbar), and cuts the throat in one swift stroke. Blood is drained.
  • Reason: respect for the life Allah gave, and as little suffering as possible.
  • Stunning: some Muslims accept meat from animals stunned first if the animal is still alive when cut; others accept only unstunned meat.
  • Fish and seafood: most Sunni scholars allow all; the Hanafi school allows only fish; Shi'a scholars allow only fish with scales, and prawns.
  • Hidden ingredients: gelatine, animal fats, alcohol in flavourings. Many Muslims look for a halal certificate.
  • Food preparation: halal and non-halal food kept apart; separate utensils where needed.
Mission 3

Alcohol and intoxicants

> "Strong drink and games of chance and idols and divining arrows are only an infamy of Satan's handiwork. Leave it aside in order that ye may succeed." (Qur'an 5:90, Pickthall)

  • The next verse gives the reason: Satan uses drink and gambling to bring enmity and to turn people from remembering Allah and from prayer (Qur'an 5:91, paraphrase).
  • The ban came in stages: drink has some benefit but more harm (2:219); do not pray while drunk (4:43); then leave it entirely (5:90).
  • The Prophet taught that every intoxicant is forbidden (Sahih Muslim, paraphrase). By qiyas this covers drugs.
  • Many Muslims also avoid selling or serving alcohol, following a hadith that blames all who make, carry, serve or sell it.
  • Issues: social events built around drinking; working in bars or restaurants; alcohol in medicines (allowed by many scholars when no alternative exists).
Quick check
?Why do many Muslims refuse to take drugs that cause a "high", although the Qur'an never names them?
Mission 3Read the source

Modesty for men and women

> "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest. That is purer for them. Lo! Allah is aware of what they do." (Qur'an 24:30, Pickthall)

> "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and be modest, and to display of their adornment only that which is apparent, and to draw their veils over their bosoms" (Qur'an 24:31, Pickthall)

  • 24:31 then lists close family before whom women need not cover their adornment.

Q1 Which command is given to both men and women?

Show answer

Lower the gaze and be modest.

Q2 Which words do scholars interpret differently?

Show answer

"that which is apparent": face and hands only, or more?

Mission 3

Modesty and dress

  • Haya (modesty): a quality of character, shown in behaviour, speech and dress.
  • Men: cover at least from navel to knee; loose clothing. The Prophet forbade gold and silk for men, permitting them to women (Sunan Abu Dawud, paraphrase).
  • Women: most scholars teach covering the whole body except face and hands in front of men outside close family.
  • Hijab means "covering": in everyday use, a headscarf. Niqab: a face veil. Jilbab, abaya: long outer garments. Chador, burqa: full coverings in some countries.
  • Both: clothes should not be tight or see-through, worn for pride, or imitate the other sex.
Mission 3Diversity

Divergent interpretations of dress

  • Majority view: 24:31 and 33:59 require women to cover their hair; the hijab is obligatory.
  • Niqab: a minority of scholars hold it obligatory; many see it as recommended or a personal choice; some say it is not required at all.
  • A minority of modern Muslims: the Qur'an commands modesty, not one garment; covering the hair reflects culture and history.
  • Reasons women give for wearing hijab: obedience to Allah, Muslim identity, being valued for character not looks, dignity.
  • Reasons some do not: they see modesty as being in the heart and behaviour; local laws or safety; personal conviction.
  • Laws differ: Iran requires women to cover their hair; France bans religious symbols such as the headscarf in state schools. In Britain, schools set uniform rules.
  • Many Muslims stress that modesty must be sincere, coming from the heart, not only from rules or pressure.
Quick check
?Two Muslim women discuss Surah 24:31. Amina wears a hijab because she understands "that which is apparent" as the face and hands. Sara wears long sleeves and loose clothes but no headscarf, saying the verse commands modesty, not one garment. Which statement is accurate?
Mission 3

Money: riba and gambling

  • Riba (usury, interest): "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury." (Qur'an 2:275, Pickthall)
  • Why: the lender gains without work or risk; debts can trap the poor; wealth is a trust from Allah.
  • Islamic finance: banks share profit and loss with customers, or buy and resell at an agreed mark-up; Islamic home finance uses leasing or joint ownership instead of an interest mortgage.
  • Some scholars allow a conventional mortgage for Muslims in non-Muslim countries when there is real need; many disagree.
  • Gambling (maysir): forbidden alongside alcohol (Qur'an 5:90). It brings money without effort, breeds enmity and can ruin families. Most Muslims avoid lotteries, betting and scratch cards.
  • Takaful: Islamic insurance based on mutual help.
Mission 3Evaluate

"Halal and haram laws are the most important part of Muslim identity."

  • For: they shape every day: food, drink, dress, money. They are visible signs of faith in a non-Muslim society. They come from the Qur'an and Sunnah.
  • Against: Tawhid and the Shahadah are the foundation; without belief, rules are empty. Identity is also shown through the ummah (the worldwide Muslim community), prayer and akhlaq (good character). Muslims differ in how strictly they apply some rules (stunning, hijab, mortgages), yet share one faith.
  • Another view: the laws are part of worship and cannot be separated from belief: obeying them is expressing Tawhid.
  • Judge it by: source of the teaching; outward signs or inner faith; daily impact; diversity of practice.
Mission check

?At a friend's house, a Muslim student is offered a new brand of sparkling drink. The label lists water, fruit juice, sugar and spices: no alcohol and no animal products. No verse or hadith names it. What would most Muslim scholars say about drinking it?

Halal is the wide default; haram is a short list drawn from the Qur'an and Sunnah, applied by scholars to food, drink, dress and money.

Mission 4

Mission 4: Muslims live in every country and speak many languages. Can they really be one community?

Make a guess: Muslims live in every country and speak many languages. Can they really be one community?

Mission 4

The ummah

  • Ummah: the worldwide community of Muslims.
  • It is based on shared faith, not on race, nation, language or class.
  • Every Muslim belongs from birth or conversion, through the Shahadah.
  • The Prophet compared believers to one body: when one part hurts, the whole body feels it (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, paraphrase).
  • The first ummah was formed in Madinah after the Hijrah: migrants from Makkah and Madinan helpers became like brothers.
  • Importance: belonging, mutual support, and a duty to care for Muslims everywhere.
Mission 4Read the source

One community

> "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." (Qur'an 3:103, Pickthall)

> "The believers are naught else than brothers. Therefore make peace between your brethren" (Qur'an 49:10, Pickthall)

> "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." (Qur'an 49:13, Pickthall)

Q1 What does 49:13 say makes a person "noblest"?

Show answer

Conduct, not nation or tribe.

Q2 What duty does 49:10 give members of the ummah?

Show answer

To make peace between fellow believers.

Mission 4

Living as one ummah

  • Worship joins Muslims: all face the qiblah (the Ka'bah) in salah; pray in Arabic; fast in the same month; meet at Hajj in the same clothes.
  • Giving: zakah and sadaqah reach Muslims in need anywhere, e.g. after floods or wars.
  • Many communities: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both see themselves as one ummah, with different schools, leaders and customs.
  • Challenges: divisions between groups and conflict between Muslim countries. Many Muslims see healing these as a duty (49:10).
Quick check
?A Muslim in Glasgow gives money at Jumu'ah prayers for families hit by an earthquake in Turkey, though she knows no one there. Which idea best explains her action?
Mission 4

Women in Islam: equal before Allah

  • Spiritual equality: men and women are created "from a single soul" (Qur'an 4:1, paraphrase) and rewarded equally:

> "Whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily we shall quicken with good life" (Qur'an 16:97, Pickthall)

  • Surah 33:35 lists the same virtues and reward for believing men and women, side by side.
  • Rights in Islamic law: to education; to own property and keep her earnings; to consent to marriage; to her mahr (marriage gift); to seek divorce (khul'); to inherit.
  • Inheritance: a daughter receives half a son's share (4:11). Scholars explain that men must provide for the family from their share, while women keep theirs.
  • Honour of mothers: asked who most deserves good treatment, the Prophet said "your mother" three times, then "your father" (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase).
  • Examples: Khadijah, a successful merchant; Aisha, a leading teacher of hadith.
Mission 4Diversity

Roles: different Muslim views

  • Traditional view: equal but different. Men lead and provide; women's first role is home and children. Supporters cite: "Men are the protectors and maintainers of women" (Qur'an 4:34, Yusuf Ali) and 2:228 (men "a degree above").
  • Reformist and Muslim feminist view: these verses describe duties in their time, not lesser worth; the Qur'an's deeper message is equal partnership (e.g. Amina Wadud, b. 1952, Qur'an and Woman, 1992).
  • Work and leadership: many Muslim women work and lead; Muslim-majority countries such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and Turkey have had women as heads of government.
  • Mosques: the Prophet said not to stop women going to mosques (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase), yet some mosques have little space for women; British campaigns seek better provision.
  • Leading prayer: most scholars teach that a woman may lead women but not a mixed congregation; a minority disagree.
  • Many Muslim women say cultural practices, not Islam, limit women in some places.
Quick check
?Which statement fairly describes the traditional Muslim view of men's and women's roles?
Mission 4

Greater jihad: living Islam in Britain

  • Greater jihad: the daily struggle (jihad) against selfishness and temptation, to live as a good Muslim. Many Muslims see it as more important than lesser jihad.
  • Lesser jihad is the outward struggle, including defending Islam under strict conditions.
  • Challenges in Britain: finding time and space for salah at school or work; Jumu'ah on a working day; long fasts in summer Ramadan; halal food when eating out; social life around alcohol; riba in loans and mortgages; dress codes; prejudice and Islamophobia.
  • Supports: mosques and Islamic schools; halal food widely sold; prayer rooms in many schools, hospitals and airports; in England, Wales and Scotland the Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination because of religion.
  • In Northern Ireland the equivalent law is the Fair Employment and Treatment Order 1998.
  • British Muslims serve as doctors, teachers, MPs, footballers and in the armed forces, while keeping their faith.
Mission 4Read the source

Living alongside others

> "Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion and drove you not out from your homes, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them. Lo! Allah loveth the just dealers." (Qur'an 60:8, Pickthall)

> "There is no compulsion in religion." (Qur'an 2:256, Pickthall)

  • Many scholars teach that Muslims living in a country must keep its laws, as an agreement they have accepted ("Fulfil your indentures", Qur'an 5:1, Pickthall), unless a law forces them to disobey Allah.

Q1 How does 60:8 tell Muslims to treat peaceful non-Muslim neighbours?

Show answer

With kindness and justice.

Q2 Why might a Muslim say keeping British law is part of Islam?

Show answer

Keeping agreements is a religious duty.

Mission 4Diversity

Different ways of being a British Muslim

  • "British and Muslim": many see no conflict; faith shapes values, and they take full part in public life.
  • More traditional communities: keep close ties to family, mosque and heritage culture; some choose Islamic schools to protect faith and language.
  • Different strictness: e.g. some take only Islamic home finance; others accept a mortgage when they see real need; some wear hijab, others do not.
  • Converts bring their own British culture into Muslim life.
  • Interfaith work: mosque open days, shared charity projects, school visits.
  • All face the same question: how to keep Islam whole while living in a society with different values.
Quick check
?A Muslim pupil asks to pray Zuhr in an empty classroom at lunchtime, and the school agrees. Which idea best describes her effort to keep her prayers at school?
Mission 4Evaluate

"It is harder to be a good Muslim in Britain than in a Muslim country."

  • For: the call to prayer is rarely heard in the streets; Id is not a public holiday; alcohol and gambling are everywhere; riba is built into finance; prejudice and media stereotypes.
  • Against: Britain protects freedom of religion by law; mosques, halal food and Islamic finance are available; living faith by choice can make it stronger.
  • Against: Muslim-majority countries have their own pressures: corruption, conflict, or rules that force outward conformity without inner faith.
  • Another view: being "good" is mainly about intention and character (greater jihad), which is a struggle everywhere.
  • Judge it by: outward practice or inner faith? Legal freedom or social support? Which kind of challenge is greater?
Mission check

?A Shi'a family and a Sunni family from different countries pray side by side at Id in a London park, then share food. Which statement best explains why both see themselves as part of one ummah?

The ummah is built on shared faith and worship; it holds many cultures and branches, and is lived out daily in places like Britain.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Why are the first words a Muslim baby hears the same as the call to prayer?

Make a guess: Why are the first words a Muslim baby hears the same as the call to prayer?

Mission 5

First words: adhan and iqamah

  • Soon after birth, the father or an elder whispers the adhan (call to prayer) into the baby's right ear.
  • Many also say the iqamah (the call that begins prayer) into the left ear.
  • So the first words the child hears are "Allahu akbar" and the Shahadah: there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger.
  • Meaning: the child is born into the ummah; life begins with Tawhid and the call to worship.
  • Tahnik: a tiny piece of softened date (or honey) is rubbed on the baby's gums, following the Prophet's practice (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase). It expresses hope for a sweet, good life.
  • Muslims believe every child is born in a natural state of submission to Allah (fitrah).
Mission 5

The seventh day: name, hair and aqiqah

  • Tasmiyah (naming): often on the 7th day. A name with a good meaning: a prophet's name, or 'Abd ("servant") with one of Allah's names, e.g. Abdullah, Abdur-Rahman.
  • Head-shaving: the baby's hair is shaved; its weight in silver (or its value) is given to the poor, following the example of Fatimah for her son Hasan.
  • Aqiqah: an animal is sacrificed in thanks for the child. In Sunni practice, often two sheep or goats for a boy and one for a girl; in Shi'a practice one for either. The meat is shared with family, friends and the poor.
  • Khitan (circumcision) of boys: a sunnah from Ibrahim. Some do it in the first week; others later in childhood.
  • Importance: thanks to Allah, a good start in the faith, and the community sharing the family's joy.
Quick check
?At an aqiqah, a family shares meat with neighbours and gives some to the poor. What does this mainly express?
Mission 5

Marriage: the nikah

  • Nikah: marriage, a contract (aqd nikah) and a sacred bond. Marriage is strongly encouraged as the Prophet's sunnah.
  • Consent: both bride and groom must freely agree; a forced marriage is not valid.
  • Offer and acceptance (ijab and qabul) are spoken before witnesses: in Sunni law two adult Muslim witnesses are required; Shi'a law recommends witnesses but does not require them.
  • Wali: a guardian, usually the bride's father, represents her in most Sunni schools; the Hanafi school allows an adult woman to contract her own marriage.
  • Mahr: a gift from the groom to the bride, agreed in the contract. It belongs to her alone.
  • The contract is signed; a short sermon (khutbah) and du'a follow, often in a mosque or at home.
Mission 5Read the source

"Love and mercy"

> "And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." (Qur'an 30:21, Pickthall)

Husbands are told to give the women they marry a "free gift of their marriage portions" (Qur'an 4:4, Pickthall).

Q1 According to 30:21, what has Allah placed between husband and wife?

Show answer

Love and mercy.

Q2 What does "free gift of their marriage portions" refer to, and whose is it?

Show answer

The mahr: it belongs to the bride.

Mission 5

Customs and the walimah

  • Before: families meet; in South Asian families, a mehndi (henna) evening for the bride.
  • During: the nikah itself is short and simple: contract, mahr, witnesses, khutbah, du'a for the couple.
  • After: the walimah, a wedding feast given by the groom's family. The Prophet told a newly married companion to give a walimah "even with one sheep" (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase).
  • Much of the rest (dress colours, music, gold) is culture, varying between countries.
  • Britain: a nikah alone is not a legal marriage. Many couples also have a civil ceremony, or marry in a mosque registered for marriages.
Quick check
?At a nikah in Leicester, the bride's father asks her in front of witnesses if she accepts the marriage, and she says yes. Why is her answer essential?
Mission 5

Divorce, khul' and remarriage

  • Divorce is allowed but a last resort; many Muslims cite a hadith calling it the most disliked of permitted things (Sunan Abu Dawud, paraphrase).
  • First, reconciliation: "appoint an arbiter from his folk and an arbiter from her folk" (Qur'an 4:35, Pickthall).
  • Talaq: divorce pronounced by the husband, followed by a waiting period (iddah, about three months, 2:228). Reconciliation is possible during it, up to twice (2:229).
  • Khul': the wife may end the marriage, usually returning the mahr ("if the woman ransom herself", Qur'an 2:229, Pickthall).
  • A qadi or, in Britain, a Shari'ah council can also dissolve a marriage at the wife's request.
  • Differences: Shi'a law needs two witnesses for talaq and rejects "triple talaq" said at once; many Muslim countries have restricted it too.
  • Remarriage is allowed for both after the iddah.
Mission 5

Death and the funeral

  • Beliefs: life is a test; death comes at the time Allah decrees (sovereignty of Allah); then judgement and akhirah (life after death).

> "Every soul will taste of death. And ye will be paid on the Day of Resurrection only that which ye have fairly earned." (Qur'an 3:185, Pickthall)

  • At death: the dying person hears or says the Shahadah; eyes are closed; mourners say "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning" (2:156).
  • Ghusl: the body is washed, by people of the same sex, usually family.
  • Kafan: wrapped in simple white cloths: rich and poor alike.
  • Salat al-janazah: funeral prayer said standing, with no bowing or prostration.
  • Burial: as soon as possible, usually within a day; never cremation. The body lies on its right side, facing Makkah.
  • Graves are simple. Mourners pray for the dead.
Mission 5Diversity

How long do Muslims mourn?

  • Weeping is allowed: the Prophet wept when his infant son Ibrahim died (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase). Loud wailing and tearing clothes are discouraged.
  • Three days of mourning for relatives (hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari); visitors bring food so the family need not cook.
  • Widows: a waiting period of "four months and ten days" (Qur'an 2:234, Pickthall), with no remarriage and simple dress.
  • Shi'a Muslims often hold majalis for the dead on the 3rd, 7th and 40th days, and yearly.
  • Some Sunni cultures, e.g. in South Asia, also mark the 40th day; other Sunni scholars reject this as bid'ah (an added practice).
  • Why the differences: different hadith collections and schools, and local culture.
  • Britain: Muslim sections in cemeteries; families ask for quick release of the body; some fly the body home for burial.
Quick check
?Why do Muslims bury the dead quickly, wrapped in simple white cloth, rather than in expensive clothes?
Mission check

?A Muslim family in Cardiff welcomes a baby girl. Her grandfather whispers the adhan, a softened date is rubbed on her gums, and on the 7th day she is named Maryam and her hair is shaved. What links all these actions?

From first words to burial, Muslim rites of passage place each life within Tawhid and the ummah, from birth to akhirah.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Every mosque has an imam: a prayer leader chosen for knowledge and character, with no priestly status.
  • The mu'azzin calls the adhan; Bilal was the first.

Mission 2

  • Id-ul-Fitr ends Ramadan: thanks to Allah, Zakat-ul-Fitr, Id prayer, new clothes, food, gifts and family.
  • Id-ul-Adha remembers Ibrahim's test (Qur'an 37:102–107) during Hajj: Id prayer, qurbani shared with family, friends and the poor; devotion, not meat, reaches Allah (22:37).

Mission 3

  • Halal (permitted) and haram (forbidden) come from the Qur'an, Sunnah and scholars; most things are halal unless forbidden.
  • Actions fall into five categories, from obligatory to forbidden.
  • Forbidden: carrion, blood, pork, meat dedicated to others than Allah (2:173), and all intoxicants (5:90); Surah 24:30–31 commands modesty for both sexes, and Muslims interpret dress differently.
  • Riba and gambling are forbidden.

Mission 4

  • The ummah is the worldwide Muslim community based on shared faith (3:103, 49:10, 49:13), shown in worship, giving and care for others.
  • Islam teaches spiritual equality of women and men, with traditional and reformist views on roles.
  • Greater jihad is the daily struggle to live as a good Muslim, including in Britain's non-Muslim society.

Mission 5

  • Birth: adhan and iqamah, tahnik, tasmiyah on the 7th day, head-shaving with charity, aqiqah, khitan for boys.
  • Marriage: nikah with consent, offer and acceptance, witnesses, contract and mahr (4:4), then walimah; love and mercy (30:21).
  • Divorce is a last resort: talaq, khul', iddah, remarriage.
  • Death: ghusl, white kafan, salat al-janazah, quick burial facing Makkah; mourning periods differ (three days; widows four months and ten days; Shi'a 3rd, 7th, 40th days).
